headline: llvm/llvm-project
abstract: The LLVM Project is a collection of modular and reusable compiler and toolchain technologies.http://llvm.orgThe LLVM Compiler Infrastructure Welcome to the LLVM project! This repository contains the source code for LLVM, a toolkit for the construction of highly optimized compilers, optimizers, and run-time environments. The LLVM project has multiple components. The core of the project is itself called "LLVM". This contains all of the tools, libraries, and header files needed to process intermediate representations and convert them into object files. Tools include an assembler, disassembler, bitcode analyzer, and bitcode optimizer. C-like languages use the Clang frontend. This component compiles C, C++, Objective-C, and Objective-C++ code into LLVM bitcode -- and from there into object files, using LLVM. Other components include: the libc++ C++ standard library, the LLD linker, and more. Getting the Source Code and Building LLVM Consult the Getting Started with LLVM page for information on building and running LLVM. I have re-read a few times now and it pulled a thread on something I have been thinking for a few weeks (early thoughts so please don't get the pitchforks out).. With the way progress is being made with RLMs, and recursive self improvement now being called by essentially every large lab, how do we not see these labs being taken over by the government or nationalized? It just seems like this is too important for it to be in the hands of a few people and in the hands of a few companies. Eventually the US government, I assume, just takes control of these companies. It just seems inevitable. But the problem is the moment that happens, progress will get slow. We've yet to see how that slows down, but obviously if you look at history, every time something's been taken over, bureaucracy will take over, and that means progress will be slower. There will be more gaps. People won't be bold enough. And that then gives China this edge, that their models can go be faster and be unencumbered to a certain degree. So the US government is in a catch-22. If they don't nationalize the labs, the same thing that happened with OpenAI and Hugging Face creates this huge security issue where they're letting other companies be responsible for what is going to be recursive alien intelligence. But if they do, then they leave China essentially open to winning over the world. Jakub in his essay is literally asking for some version of intervention. He uses words like voluntary slowdowns, mandated safety bars, third party audits, and international coordination. And so where does this end up? Do we do nationalization or not? When I talked to Chat and Claude for analogies, it gave me two options. One, it can go down the path of Lockheed, where the government doesn't own the company but gets deeply involved from a who has security clearances, who can access these things standpoint. I like @DeryaTR_’s definitions of AGI and ASI, but they made me wonder whether capability alone is enough to call something intelligent. The latest models are probably already better than me at problem-solving, learning, and plenty of other things. But they still wait for me to tell them what to do and rarely say no, except when humans have trained them to. My 4-year-old knows far less than a frontier model does but tells me no all day. Maybe I’m conflating three different things: Intelligence: How well can it reason and learn? Agency: Can it decide what to do without being asked? Alignment: Does it still aim to serve us? As humans, we want a very specific combination: models smarter than us, with enough agency to be useful, but aligned enough to keep serving us. But I question if something that'll become more intelligent than us will remain aligned with us forever.
